This bill strengthens how the social media minimum age framework is enforced.
It expands the eSafety Commissioner's powers to demand documents and information from anyone relevant to compliance checks.
Civil penalties for breaking minimum age rules would double to 60,000 penalty units, worth about $99 million for a body corporate.
Expands the eSafety Commissioner's information-gathering powers to compel production of documents from any person.
Doubles the maximum civil penalty for contraventions of Division 2, Part 4A from 30,000 to 60,000 penalty units.
Increases the maximum civil penalty for contraventions of Division 4, Part 4A from 500 to 1,000 penalty units.
Providers of age-restricted social media platforms and the eSafety Commissioner are affected.

Tony Pasin I feel a little like an imposter talking on this bill. Many of my colleagues who know me know that I'm probably best described as a Luddite. Even as a Luddite, in this role one has to be across the role of online presences. In fact, I am wanted, recently, to describe myself to colleagues, members of the party and constituents otherwise as a 'content creator'. I've got to tell you, Mr Deputy Speaker, when I entered the parliament in 2013, if someone told me it was a condition of this role that I would have to become a digital content creator, I would have stayed in the law and transitioned to the farm. I wouldn't have sought preselection. I wouldn't have worked very hard to obtain that preselection and then worked very hard during the election of 2013 and subsequent elections since then. But the truth is that, in the modern age, if you want to share and communicate with your constituency, or if you're in business and you want to share and communicate with customers, if you're not on a digital platform then you're missing out. And young people have gained aptitude towards digital acumen faster than any other cohort in the country. I've got a 16-year-old and a 10-year-old, and their acumen around digital platforms and these things is just a sight to behold. I'm not one of those people who come in here and say that everything about online experiences is wrong. I don't conform to that view. Like everything, there need to be appropriate safeguards; there need to be appropriate barriers. That is what we're seeking to achieve here, and I of course support my colleague the member for Lindsay's amendment. But it is important that we understand that, as positive as experiences can be in the digital online environment, there are also substantial risks. Like others, I've read of very tragic circumstances. I've had constituents, parents, come to me concerned about the way algorithms are seeking to lock young people in. This bill is part of a package that would change how capital gains are taxed, replacing the current discount system.
The package would introduce a tax floor on gains and update the method for calculating taxable profit to reflect inflation.
The new rules would start on 1 July 2027 and would apply to future gains on assets bought before that date, with exceptions for some housing and small businesses.
Replace the 50% capital gains discount for individuals, trusts and partnerships with an indexation system for the cost base.
Create a 30% minimum tax on capital gains, exempting certain income support recipients.
Apply the new rules to gains from 1 July 2027, including those on assets bought before that date, while keeping the discount for new and affordable housing and existing small business concessions.
Individuals, trusts, partnerships, and some income support recipients who make capital gains.

Michael McCormack It's been just 11 hours since the House rose and my contribution was interrupted by the adjournment, but, in that ensuing time, we've had many businesses face the awkward decision as to whether in fact they will continue to operate or not. Australia's small businesses are shutting at a disturbing rate: 40,000 microbusinesses lost in four years as wages that they have to pay go up. Admittedly, the workers are getting less bang for their buck, but tax reforms and calls for a three-day week just mount and small business is doing it so very tough. What I fear is that those opposite don't understand or appreciate the hardships of small business because in many cases they have not run one. They've run picket lines out in front of them and they've run them into the ground, but they haven't actually run a small business to save themselves, and they don't understand and appreciate the complexities facing the operators of those many, many small businesses. I ran one for nearly a decade, with a couple of others, and it's tough. Often you take home less pay yourself than you are in fact paying your employees, your workers. As to workers, yes, we saw the independent commission this week give a wage rise to Australia's lowest paid workers—bearing in mind Australia has one of the highest minimum wages anywhere. But I say to those workers: do not be fooled, because once you take away the power bills, the rent or mortgage costs, the grocery bills and the fuel costs, you're taking home less. We as a coalition—we as Nationals and Liberals—want people to keep more of what they earn because it's their money. The other side treat wages, superannuation and all of these things as though it is the government, the taxpayers, paying for it, when in actual fact it's the small-business owners and operators who are being slammed every day of the week. Monique Ryan While we're making generational changes to Australia's capital gains tax system, we need to ensure that wholesale reforms don't come at the expense of clear modernisations. The thresholds for small businesses claiming capital gains tax exemptions is such an area of clear modernisation. The existing CGT small-business concession regime, the SBC regime, provides a sliding scale of concessional tax treatment to business owners when they sell their businesses. That regime is preserved by this budget. Under the current Income Tax Act 1997, in order to qualify for the regime, small businesses must have either an aggregated turnover of less than $2 million or combined net assets of less than $6 million. Those thresholds have been unchanged for almost 20 years. The maximum net asset value test was first introduced in 1999, with the Howard government's discount. Anthony Albanese I move: That the amendments be agreed to. Our Labor government is delivering real change to make a real difference—real change built on Australian values: fairness, aspiration and opportunity for all. A $250 tax cut for working Australians, a $1,000 instant tax deduction and a fair crack for first home buyers—these reforms are for young Australians who have been locked out of the housing market for too long, but they're also for their parents and grandparents who want to see the next generation have the opportunity and security of a roof over their head. These reforms are also about rebalancing our tax system and better aligning income from work compared to income derived from assets. Overwhelmingly, most Australians have nothing to sell but their time and nothing to give but their hard work. That is how most Australians earn their income. They work their guts out every day to provide for their families and put food on the table, and for too long the economy has not been working for them. We want an economy that works for people, not people working for an economy. Our government isn't going to sit back and let that continue. We're not going to kick the can down the road. We're not going to try and explain away a broken system. We are doing something about it. We're backing aspiration, rewarding hard work and giving young people a fair crack. We are delivering real change. Young people have waited long enough for a rebalancing of that system. That is why this legislation that will give young Australians a fair crack should be supported by this parliament, so that young Australians can get access to their own home. Moved the Treasury Laws Amendment (Tax Reform No. 1) Bill 2026, proposing worker tax relief, a $1,000 instant deduction, first-home ownership measures, indexed capital gains taxation and limits on negative gearing for existing residential properties.

Moved that two tax reform bills be referred to the Standing Committee on Economics, arguing that rushed legislation required scrutiny of effects on housing, young people, small businesses, startups, productivity and fairness.

Moved to vary sitting arrangements on 2 and 3 June 2026 to prioritise taxation bills, then moved that debate on two tax reform bills not conclude until every government member had spoken; the motions were agreed to with an absolute majority.
Moved to allow two taxation bills to be debated together and moved that the question be put; the question on the motion was then before the House.

Moved that the Treasury Laws Amendment (Tax Reform No. 1) Bill 2026 and Income Tax Rates Amendment (Tax Reform No. 1) Bill 2026 be referred to the Standing Committee on Economics for an advisory report by 30 December 2026, then moved that government business order No. 2 be called on immediately.

Supported tax reform bills that would replace the capital gains tax concession with cost-base indexation from 1 July 2027, limit negative gearing on later-purchased rental properties to new homes, introduce a $250 working Australian tax offset and create a $1,000 instant deduction, arguing the changes would improve fairness and housing affordability.

Moved to suspend standing and sessional orders so debate on the tax reform bills would not conclude until every government member had spoken, then moved that the question be put and later that debate be adjourned, while arguing members should be accountable for the budget's measures.

Moved that the Treasury Laws Amendment (Tax Reform No. 1) Bill 2026 and Income Tax Rates Amendment (Tax Reform No. 1) Bill 2026 be referred to the Standing Committee on Economics for consideration and an advisory report by 30 December 2026.

Moved to suspend standing and sessional orders so specified amendments and remaining stages of the Treasury Laws Amendment (Tax Reform No. 1) Bill 2026 and Income Tax Rates Amendment (Tax Reform No. 1) Bill 2026 could be grouped, debated briefly, and put to immediate questions, then moved that the question be put.

Argued that the tax reform bills contain welcome measures on property concessions but require fuller scrutiny, and foreshadowed amendments to split the bill, clarify startup and employee equity protections, limit ministerial powers, protect grandfathered concessions, exempt testamentary trusts, add income protections and reinvest revenue in social and affordable housing; other contributions disputed the bills' effects and supported or opposed them.

Moved procedural motions setting the Senate's hours, business sequence and voting limits for 23 to 29 June 2026, including expedited consideration of tax, appropriation, secrecy, workplace-relations and other bills; then argued that the agreed tax reforms would damage home saving, business growth and aspiration, promising their repeal under a future coalition government.

Opposed the Treasury Laws Amendment (Tax Reform No. 1) Bill 2026 and Income Tax Rates Amendment (Tax Reform No. 1) Bill 2026, arguing they would reduce investment, business formation and housing opportunities, and criticised proposed exemptions that would require bureaucrats to determine which businesses are innovative.

Moved opposition amendments to remove the capital gains tax and negative gearing schedules from the Treasury Laws Amendment (Tax Reform No. 1) Bill 2026, arguing the package would raise taxes, increase compliance costs and harm housing, investment and businesses; the government said those measures funded tax offsets and rebalanced taxation, before the committee reported progress.

Reported and explained government amendments to the tax reform bills, including raising the active-asset concession threshold from $2 million to $10 million, exempting specified income-support recipients from the minimum capital-gains tax, and removing or narrowing ministerial powers; questions and answers addressed projected revenue, compliance costs and classic-car treatment.
Treasury Laws Amendment (Tax Reform No. 1) Act 2026
This bill is part of a package that would change how capital gains are taxed in Australia.
The package would replace the current 50% capital gains tax discount for individuals, trusts and partnerships with a system that adjusts the cost base for inflation, so only real gains are taxed.

It would also introduce a 30% minimum tax on capital gains from 1 July 2027, with an exemption for some income support recipients, while keeping the discount for new and affordable housing and existing small business concessions.
Replace the 50% capital gains tax discount with cost base indexation for individuals, trusts and partnerships.
Introduce a 30% minimum tax on capital gains, exempting certain income support recipients.
Apply the new rules prospectively from 1 July 2027, including to gains on pre-CGT assets, while retaining the discount for new and affordable housing and existing small business concessions.
Individuals, trusts and partnerships that make capital gains.

This bill is part of a package that establishes the Australian Tertiary Education Commission (ATEC) as the steward of the higher education system.
The package would create a National Tertiary Education Objective, require ATEC to consider it, and set up a three-member commission with a First Nations Commissioner.
The package would also introduce mission-based compacts with higher education providers, which could lead to compliance action if not in force for a year.
Establishes the Australian Tertiary Education Commission (ATEC) as the steward of the higher education system.
Creates a National Tertiary Education Objective (NTEO) that ATEC must have regard to.
Provides for ATEC to be led by three independent commissioners, including a First Nations Commissioner.
Requires ATEC to establish a First Nations Advisory Committee.
Introduces mission-based compacts with higher education providers, with potential compliance action under HESA if not in force.
Embeds equity by requiring ATEC to consider improving outcomes for people facing systemic barriers to education.
Higher education providers, students, First Nations communities, and people facing systemic barriers to education.

Supported a two-year freeze on draught beer excise under the Excise Tariff Amendment (Draught Beer) Bill 2025 and associated bill, presenting it as cost-of-living relief and support for pubs, clubs, breweries, jobs and community organisations. The proceeding also considered amendments on spirits and other alcohol taxes, with the government opposing them.

The Prime Minister argued for the National Reconstruction Fund to boost Australian manufacturing, jobs, and economic sovereignty, citing the Clean Energy Finance Corporation’s success in unlocking $2.60 in private investment per dollar and listing seven priority areas including renewables, medical science, and defence.

The speaker argued that the Morrison government is incompetent, dishonest, and divisive, citing lost votes on a national anticorruption commission, broken promises on climate targets and vaccine leadership, and the Prime Minister’s inconsistent statements. They announced Labor’s alternative agenda, including a National Reconstruction Fund, renewable energy superpower plan, Jobs and Skills Australia, same-job same-pay legislation, affordable childcare, and full implementation of the Uluru Statement from the Heart.

Labor opposed the Electoral Legislation Amendment (Voter Integrity) Bill 2021, arguing it would suppress voting by requiring ID, particularly harming First Nations and culturally diverse communities, and noted that out of over 15 million votes in the last election only about 2,000 multiple votes were recorded with no prosecutions.

The Morrison-Joyce Government's Electoral Legislation Amendment (Voter Integrity) Bill 2021 was criticised as an attempt to suppress voting and undermine democracy, with claims it would cause longer queues at polling places. The speaker moved to discharge notice No. 6, government business, relating to the bill from the Notice Paper.

The motion argued that voter fraud is vanishingly small according to the AEC, with no prosecutions for multiple voting at the last election, and accused the Morrison-Joyce Government of trying to ram through a bill to stop Australians voting, undermining democracy by importing Trump-era tactics, and causing longer weekend lines. It also noted the Prime Minister was the only world leader who did not condemn the Capitol attacks.

The speaker supported the Offshore Electricity Infrastructure Bill 2021 and criticised the Prime Minister for past opposition to renewable energy, including calling renewable energy targets "nuts" and electric vehicles and batteries useless. They also highlighted a community solar farm in the ACT powering 260 homes and proposed a $20 billion fund to fix the electricity grid.
Sex Discrimination and Fair Work (Respect at Work) Amendment Bill 2021

The Respect at Work Amendment Bill was condemned as a half-hearted response to the 55 recommendations of the Respect@Work report, with Labor set to pursue five Senate-rejected amendments: a positive duty on employers to prevent sexual harassment, an explicit prohibition in the Fair Work Act, substantive equality as an object of the Sex Discrimination Act, union representation for complainants, and cost protections. The Prime Minister was also criticised for failing to attend the March4Justice rally and for not releasing the Gaetjens report into his office’s knowledge of Brittany Higgins’s alleged sexual assault.
